facts.summary: Louisiana has no state minimum wage law, so the federal FLSA rate of $7.25/hour applies, and state law bars local governments from setting a higher rate.
facts.notes: Louisiana enacts no independent minimum wage; RS 23:642 preempts local minimum-wage ordinances so the federal $7.25 governs statewide. Verify the federal rate remains $7.25 for 2026.

facts.summary: Louisiana has no state overtime law, so the federal FLSA standard governs: non-exempt employees are owed 1.5x pay for hours over 40 in a workweek, and there is no daily overtime.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
facts.notes: Louisiana enacts no independent overtime statute; the federal FLSA weekly-overtime rule and white-collar exemptions (including the federal salary level) apply statewide. Verify no legislative change for 2026.

facts.summary: Beyond the federal Title VII/ADA/ADEA classes, Louisiana's Employment Discrimination Law expressly protects military status and natural, protective, or cultural hairstyle (CROWN Act).
facts.notes: RS 23:332 lists race, color, religion, sex, national origin, military status, and natural/protective/cultural hairstyle. Louisiana also protects sickle cell trait (RS 23:352) and pregnancy/childbirth (RS 23:341-342) in separate sections not verified via official URL here.

facts.summary: Louisiana's Employment Discrimination Law applies only to employers with 20 or more employees, a higher threshold than federal Title VII's 15.
facts.notes: Covers employers with 20+ employees for each working day in 20+ calendar weeks in the current or preceding year. This is narrower than federal (15+), so smaller employers may still be reached only by federal law.

facts.summary: Louisiana's whistleblower statute bars employer reprisal against an employee who, in good faith, discloses, testifies about, or refuses to participate in a workplace practice that violates state law.
facts.notes: Remedies include compensatory damages, back pay, benefits, reinstatement, reasonable attorney fees, and court costs. Protection generally requires an actual violation of state law and prior notice to the employer.

facts.summary: A suit to recover unpaid wages or salary is subject to a three-year liberative prescription (statute of limitations) under Louisiana Civil Code article 3494.
facts.notes: Article 3494 sets a 3-year prescription for actions to recover compensation for services rendered, including salaries, wages, and commissions.

facts.value: 1 year prescriptive period (suspended up to 6 months during EEOC/LCHR review)
facts.summary: A Louisiana employment-discrimination lawsuit must be filed within one year, but that period is suspended (tolled) during any EEOC or Louisiana Commission on Human Rights review for up to six additional months.
facts.notes: This is the deadline to file suit, not merely an administrative charge; RS 23:303(C) also requires 30 days' written notice to the employer before suit. Maximum suspension is 6 months. Federal EEOC 180/300-day charge deadlines still apply separately.

facts.value: next regular payday or within 15 days of separation, whichever is first
facts.summary: On discharge or resignation, Louisiana requires payment of final wages by the next regular payday or no later than 15 days after separation, whichever occurs first.
facts.notes: Accrued, unused vacation counts as an amount due if the employee was eligible and it was earned. Failure to pay can trigger penalty wages and attorney fees under RS 23:632. Federal law has no comparable final-pay timing rule.
